title: Graphene quantum dot–gold nanocomposites for cancer biomarker and cell detection: interfacial design and analytical reliability
content: Graphene quantum dot–gold (GQD–Au) nanocomposites support the optical and electrochemical detection of cancer-associated biomarkers and cells; however, their analytical performance is difficult to evaluate when the material composition, recognition chemistry, and assay configuration change simultaneously. This review critically examines these platforms through a framework connecting material identity, interfacial organization, recognition-induced perturbations, and measurement validity. It distinguishes direct GQD–Au hybrids from supported and multicomponent architectures and compares nucleic-acid, protein, and intact-cell assays according to the constituent function, response mechanism, calibration, and biological-matrix testing. The reviewed evidence reveals architectural diversity concentrated around a limited set of targets, particularly carcinoembryonic antigen, while supporting materials, reporter placement, and capture procedures frequently contribute to the measured response. An approximately ninety-fold difference reported between buffer and serum detection limits within one prostate-specific-antigen platform illustrates the importance of matrix-specific validation. Multiplexed measurements demonstrate channel discrimination, while low cell-concentration limits require interpretation alongside specimen volume and capture recovery. The contribution of this review is an evidence-based organization of design relationships that separates demonstrated assay behavior from proposed mechanisms and inferred diagnostic utility. It identifies matched component controls, independent fabrication, reference-method comparison, and representative specimen testing as the priorities for establishing transferable performance. GQD–Au development should therefore be evaluated through interpretable recognition–transduction relationships and measurement validation under intended-use conditions, with the detection limits considered as one component of analytical quality.
